evidence_quotes.quote: Al 2022, el acueducto de estudio contaba con 650 abonados (cubriendo una población aproximada de 2265 personas) que cancelan una cuota mensual de 2000 colones (equivalente a aproximadamente 4 USD al tipo de cambio promedio de 2025). Sin embargo, esta tarifa resulta insuficiente para la sostenibilidad y funcionamiento óptimo de las condiciones del acueducto.

Según indicó, la comunidad no quiere colocar medidores y tampoco subir la tarifa plana que cobran, lo que dificulta en la práctica a las personas del comité poder hacer las mejorar realmente necesarias y dar mantenimientos adecuados (desinfectar, comprar insumos y poder asegurar y pagarle al fontanero que debe ser calificado).

Lo anterior, sumado a la falta de información financiera que debería brindar la administración del acueducto al AyA, hace que el acueducto que abastece la comunidad sea catalogado por el Sistema de Apoyo y Gestión de ASADAS (SAGA) en categoría C (categoría más baja). Aunque reconoció que la institución ha hecho un esfuerzo para cambiar el sistema y categorizar de forma separada a las comunidades indígenas debido a que presentan situaciones atípicas, tales como normativas diferenciadas y falta de personerías jurídicas que permitan respaldar “el manejo de fondos públicos, donaciones, todo eso de tuberías y cosas de ese tipo”

Las fuentes primarias incluyen expedientes institucionales del Instituto Costarricense de Acueductos y Alcantarillados (AyA) que compila el trabajo de sus diferentes unidades estratégica de negocios (UEN) y del Ministerio de Salud, informes técnicos, análisis de calidad del agua, normativa, registros de giras de campo, transcripciones de dos talleres comunitarios y entrevistas cualitativas realizadas a actores clave, tanto institucionales como comunitarios.

Entre 2011 y 2012, persistieron los problemas de mantenimiento del acueducto, especialmente en la captación de agua y almacenamiento, lo que resultó en que los análisis del agua distribuida indicaron que no era apta para consumo humano (AyA, 2011). Durante este periodo, el acueducto abastecía a 244 hogares en Amubri, 160 en Suiri, 80 en Cachabri, y cuatro centros educativos, todos sin medidores.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community drinking-water service access, aqueduct coverage, system sustainability, and potability in the Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri (and neighbouring Cachabri and Suiri sharing the aqueduct) in Talamanca, Costa Rica, from 1990 to 2022.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it examines state water policies, AyA and Ministry of Health governance, and community water management. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it specifically analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing community water service sustainability and access: (1) tariff and cost-recovery rules requiring communal aqueducts (ASADAs) to self-finance solely through user tariffs without state subsidies, alongside disputes over flat monthly tariffs (2,000 vs. 500 colones) and metering refusal; (2) administrative reporting and regulatory classification rules under AyA's SAGA system (placing the aqueduct in the lowest category C for lacking financial reports); (3) legal documentation/status requirements (lack of personería jurídica in Indigenous territories restricting receipt of public funds, donations, and piping); and (4) centralized sanitary orders and chlorination mandates interacting with Indigenous sociocultural norms and accommodation efforts.
criterion_notes.c3: Original qualitative socio-historical empirical case study (approved by the University of Costa Rica Ethics Committee under project B9314) combining primary archival institutional files (AyA Expediente 7-4-4 Amubri-Cachabri-Suiri and Ministry of Health records, 1990-2022), microbiological water-quality testing (INISA 2019 and 2021), two community workshops, and qualitative interviews with institutional officials and Bribri residents.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household/subscriber connection counts (230-254 households in 2003; 484 households and 4 schools across Amubri, Suiri, and Cachabri in 2011-2012; 650 subscribers serving ~2,265 residents in 2022), tariff affordability and payment compliance/fragmentation (Suiri splitting off over tariff levels), maintenance continuity, seasonal source shortages, and drinking-water potability/fecal coliform contamination.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri and shared aqueduct subscribers/households in Talamanca, Costa Rica), exposure (centralized ASADA regulatory, legal-personality, financial-reporting, sanitary, and tariff cost-recovery rules), outcome (service sustainability, subscriber coverage, tariff compliance, and water potability), and study design (qualitative socio-historical case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish with an English abstract. Per Criterion 10, Spanish is eligible because translation from the clean, accessible PDF full text is feasible and the study provides important empirical socio-legal evidence on Indigenous water service regulation, legal personality barriers, and cost-recovery rules; translation method and translator should be logged in extraction_note during data extraction.

study_design: Qualitative socio-historical case study (archival review of institutional files, qualitative interviews, community workshops, and microbiological water-quality sampling)
population_and_sample: Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri (and neighbouring Cachabri and Suiri sharing the aqueduct) in Talamanca, Limón Province, Costa Rica (aqueduct/ASADA system serving 650 subscribers / ~2,265 residents in 2022; qualitative interviews with institutional officials and community residents, two community workshops, water samples, and institutional case files from 1990 to 2022)
exposure: State water governance and delegated communal aqueduct (ASADA) regulatory and cost-recovery rules administered by AyA and the Ministry of Health, including mandatory self-financing via tariffs without state subsidies, metering, financial reporting and SAGA categorization, legal personality (personería jurídica) requirements for receiving public funds/donations, and sanitary/chlorination mandates
outcome: Community drinking-water service coverage and continuity (650 subscribers / ~2,265 residents in 2022), tariff payment compliance and affordability conflicts, infrastructure maintenance sustainability, and microbiological potability of distributed water
rationale: This qualitative socio-historical empirical case study examines household and community drinking-water supply in the Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri, Costa Rica (1990-2022). Beyond general governance tensions, it analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms under Criterion 2 (2026-10-13 clarification), including the strict tariff cost-recovery regime without state subsidies for communal aqueducts, flat-tariff and metering disputes, financial reporting rules resulting in lowest SAGA category C status, lack of legal personality (personería jurídica) restricting access to public funds and donated materials, and centralized sanitary enforcement. Primary empirical methods (archival files, qualitative interviews, community workshops, and microbiological water sampling) and service-relevant outcomes (connections, tariff payment/affordability, system maintenance, and potability) are clearly reported, and full-text translation from Spanish is feasible per Criterion 10.
